fields.text: I know I need to do this, but I keep putting off taking the first step.
I start the task, but after a while my mind drifts to something else.
When I need to move from one task to the next, it takes me time to shift gears.
In the middle of a multi-step task, I sometimes forget exactly where I was.
When a task has several steps, it can be hard for me to work out the right order.
I start several tasks, but getting them all the way to the finish can be difficult.
Sometimes I react before I have had a chance to think.

fields.conceptualThreshold: When intended actions are repeatedly started substantially later than intended and the delay is maladaptive or has meaningful consequences, Procrastination may be a useful educational description.
fields.singleEventCaution: One delayed start is not enough to establish a recurring Procrastination pattern.
fields.examples: Example that does not meet the pattern: one important task starts late. Example that may fit educationally: important intended tasks are repeatedly started late and this repeatedly creates meaningful negative consequences.

fields.conceptualThreshold: When performance or engagement varies meaningfully across repeated occasions, contexts, or time, Performance Variability may be a useful educational description.
fields.singleEventCaution: One bad day or one unusually productive day is insufficient. Everyday inconsistency must not be treated as equivalent to laboratory reaction-time variability findings.
fields.examples: Example that does not meet the pattern: performance is poor once. Example that may fit educationally: performance is repeatedly much more stable in some contexts than others across multiple occasions.

fields.label: Sleep / physical state
fields.explanation: Insufficient sleep, fatigue, or another temporary physical state can affect attention, energy, inhibition, and task performance.
fields.safeWording: Current physical state can also affect this behaviour.

fields.label: Acute stress
fields.explanation: Acute stress can compete with cognitive resources and alter attention, working memory, flexibility, and emotional responding.
fields.safeWording: Acute stress can produce similar difficulties without establishing ADHD.

fields.label: Anxiety / emotional distress
fields.explanation: Anxiety or emotional distress can make concentration, task engagement, organization, and pausing before reaction more difficult.
fields.safeWording: Emotional difficulties can produce similar patterns; this does not mean anxiety is the explanation for a specific person.

fields.label: Low mood
fields.explanation: Low mood can reduce energy, engagement, concentration, and follow-through in ways that may resemble some of these behaviours.
fields.safeWording: Low mood is one possible non-ADHD contributor, not a conclusion about the user.

fields.label: Burnout
fields.explanation: Sustained overload or burnout can reduce available energy and cognitive capacity for starting, sustaining, organizing, tracking, and completing tasks.
fields.safeWording: Burnout can create similar difficulties and should not be ranked against ADHD by this product.

fields.label: Grief
fields.explanation: Grief can temporarily affect attention, memory, energy, emotional load, and everyday task functioning.
fields.safeWording: Grief may contribute to similar difficulties; the product does not determine whether it applies.

fields.label: Task design
fields.explanation: Unclear definitions, excessive complexity, poor sequencing, or ambiguous completion criteria can make a task difficult regardless of ADHD.
fields.safeWording: The structure of the task itself may contribute.

fields.label: Workload
fields.explanation: Excessive or competing workload can increase cognitive and organizational demand and leave tasks delayed, unstable, or unfinished.
fields.safeWording: Excessive workload is a possible contributor and is not evidence of ADHD.

fields.label: Environment / distraction
fields.explanation: Noise, interruptions, competing stimuli, or frequent forced transitions can make attention and task continuity more difficult.
fields.safeWording: Some environments make this behaviour harder even without ADHD.

fields.label: Skill gap
fields.explanation: An unfamiliar process, missing knowledge, or insufficient practice can make starting, tracking, sequencing, switching, or completing a task harder.
fields.safeWording: Difficulty may reflect missing knowledge or experience rather than a regulation problem.

fields.label: Ordinary motivation / preference
fields.explanation: Low personal relevance, ordinary dislike of a task, or competing priorities can reduce engagement without implying a clinical problem.
fields.safeWording: Not every difficult or uninteresting task reflects a clinical problem.

fields.label: Physical illness
fields.explanation: Physical illness can alter energy, concentration, memory, and everyday functioning.
fields.safeWording: Physical illness can produce similar difficulties; the product does not infer whether this applies to a user.

fields.label: Medication / substance effects
fields.explanation: Medication or substance effects can alter attention, arousal, inhibition, memory, or energy in ways that may affect these behaviours.
fields.safeWording: Medication or substance effects are a possible contributor where relevant; this product does not make medication or substance-use judgments.

fields.title: Procrastination / Urgency
fields.orderedSteps: Starting is delayed → Repeated maladaptive delay may form a Procrastination pattern → The deadline becomes closer → Urgency / Time Pressure increases → Consequences or rewards become more immediate → Reward / Delay Processing changes → Starting or Sustaining may change → A task may sometimes be completed under pressure → Future reliance on urgency may be reinforced
fields.explanation: This loop is an educational synthesis showing how delayed Starting and Procrastination can alter future urgency, which can in turn change reward immediacy and task engagement.
fields.caution: This loop is not universal, not ADHD-specific, and not a proven single neurobiological mechanism.

fields.title: Functional Difficulty → Stress
fields.orderedSteps: A Behaviour or Pattern difficulty occurs → Difficulty may matter in a Functional Domain → Stress / Emotional Load may increase → Regulatory demands may increase → Behaviour may become less stable → Further functional difficulty may occur
fields.explanation: This loop is a transdiagnostic educational synthesis: functional difficulty may increase stress, and stress may increase demands on regulation systems that can affect subsequent behaviour.
fields.caution: The relationship is probabilistic and transdiagnostic. The application must not infer a deterministic stress cycle for a specific person.

fields.label: Predominantly Inattentive Presentation
fields.description: A current ADHD presentation in which the formal inattention symptom domain predominates under clinical diagnostic criteria.

fields.label: Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Presentation
fields.description: A current ADHD presentation in which the formal hyperactivity–impulsivity symptom domain predominates under clinical diagnostic criteria.

fields.label: Combined Presentation
fields.description: A current ADHD presentation in which formal symptoms from both inattention and hyperactivity–impulsivity domains meet clinical criteria.

fields.label: Historical ADD terminology
fields.description: ADD is an older diagnostic term still commonly encountered, especially in references to predominantly inattentive ADHD. It is not a separate current disorder, a fourth presentation, or a current canonical synonym for ADHD.

fields.text: This is an educational model of ADHD-related concepts and research. It does not diagnose ADHD or provide individualized medical advice.
Connections show possible associations or influences, not universal causal pathways.
This behaviour alone does not indicate ADHD and may have several different explanations.
Similar difficulties can occur for reasons unrelated to ADHD.
One event is not enough to establish a recurring pattern.
A difficulty in this area does not automatically mean clinically significant impairment.
ADHD presentations are based on formal clinical symptom domains, not this explanatory graph.
Research findings describe group-level tendencies and do not define an individual profile.
